chapters.n: A new era begins. Moses is gone, and the Lord speaks directly to Joshua, who had served as Moses’ assistant for forty years. His name means “Jehovah saves” — the Hebrew form of the name Jesus.

f.g: Hebrew Yehoshua; Greek Iēsous — the same name as Jesus.

chapters.n: God’s message is simple: Moses is dead — now get up and lead the people across the Jordan. Grief gives way to action.
Wherever they walk, God has already given them the land, just as promised to Moses. Their part is to step forward in faith.

f.w: Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon

chapters.n: The promised borders reach from the southern desert to Lebanon, east to the Euphrates, and west to the Mediterranean.

f.g: Here a general name for Syria and the lands to the north.

chapters.n: God promises Joshua what he gave Moses: no one will withstand him, and God will never abandon him.

f.w: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee
as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee

chapters.n: The first of three calls to courage. Joshua’s task is to lead Israel in dividing the promised land.

f.w: Be strong and of a good courage

chapters.n: Courage is needed most for obedience. Strength here means keeping God’s law without swerving — the true key to success.

f.w: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left

chapters.n: Joshua must keep the law on his lips and ponder it day and night. Scripture study is the foundation of prosperity in God’s sense.

f.g: Meditate = murmur or recite quietly while reflecting.

chapters.n: “Have I not commanded you?” Courage is a commandment, grounded in the promise that God goes everywhere with us.

f.w: be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed

chapters.n: Joshua immediately acts, giving orders to the officers.

f.g: Administrative leaders, perhaps scribes or organizers.

chapters.n: Gather food — in three days they will cross the Jordan. Faith includes practical preparation.
Joshua turns to the two and a half tribes that had already received land east of the Jordan.
He reminds them of their promise to Moses: God has given them rest and land.
Their families and herds stay behind, but the warriors must cross armed and help the other tribes.
They can return home only after their brothers also have rest. Covenant people don’t settle down while others still struggle.

f.w: Until the LORD have given your brethren rest

chapters.n: The eastern tribes — and all Israel — pledge complete obedience: “Whatever you command, we’ll do; wherever you send, we’ll go.”

f.w: whithersoever thou sendest us, we will go

chapters.n: They will follow Joshua as they followed Moses, and they pray that God will be with him in the same way.

f.w: only the LORD thy God be with thee

chapters.n: They even back his authority with the strongest penalty, and they echo God’s own words back to him: “Be strong and courageous!”

f.w: only be strong and of a good courage

chapters.n: From the camp at Shittim, Joshua secretly sends two scouts to Jericho, the fortified city guarding the way into Canaan. They lodge with a woman named Rahab, whose house was a natural place for strangers to stay unnoticed.

f.g: “Acacias” — Israel’s camp on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan.
Some ancient interpreters suggested “innkeeper,” but the Hebrew zonah normally means prostitute.

chapters.n: Word reaches Jericho’s king that Israelite spies have arrived that night.

f.g: A local city-state ruler; Canaan had many such kings.

chapters.n: The king demands that Rahab hand them over.
Rahab hides the men and admits visitors came, but claims she didn’t know where they were from.

f.w: I wist not whence they were
f.g: Wist = knew. “I didn’t know where they came from.”

chapters.n: She says they left at dusk before the city gate closed and urges the soldiers to chase them. Her deception protected God’s messengers; scripture praises her faith, not the lie itself.

f.g: City gates were closed at nightfall for security.

chapters.n: In truth, she had hidden them on her flat roof under flax stalks drying in the sun.

f.g: Flax was harvested in spring and dried on rooftops to make linen — fitting the Passover season of Joshua 5.

chapters.n: The searchers head toward the Jordan crossings, and the city gate is shut behind them — trapping the spies inside but also keeping pursuers out.

f.g: Shallow crossing places in the river.

chapters.n: Before the men settle for the night, Rahab goes up to speak with them.

f.g: Flat roofs served as private living space.

chapters.n: Rahab’s confession of faith: “I know the Lord has given you the land.” A Canaanite woman shows more faith than Israel’s spies did forty years earlier.

f.w: I know that the LORD hath given you the land

chapters.n: News of the Red Sea crossing and the defeat of Sihon and Og had reached Jericho forty years later.

f.w: the LORD dried up the water of the Red sea

chapters.n: Rahab’s testimony reaches its peak: Israel’s God is the God of heaven and earth. She acknowledges him as the true God.

f.w: he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath

chapters.n: She asks the spies to swear by the Lord to show her family the same loyal kindness she showed them, with a sure sign.
Her request is for her whole family: parents, siblings, and all they have.
The spies pledge their own lives for hers, on condition she keeps their mission secret. They promise to treat her with loyalty and faithfulness.

f.g: “May we die if you don’t live.”

chapters.n: Her house was built into the city wall, so she lowered them out a window by a rope. Archaeologists note houses were sometimes built into casemate walls.

f.g: Her house formed part of the city’s fortification.

chapters.n: She advises them to hide in the hills west of Jericho for three days, while the pursuers search toward the river.

f.g: The rugged hills west of Jericho, full of caves.

chapters.n: The spies set terms so they won’t be guilty of breaking the oath.

f.g: We will be free from guilt.

chapters.n: The sign: tie the scarlet cord in the window, and gather all your family inside. Many Christians see the red cord as a symbol of Christ’s saving blood, like the Passover blood on the doorposts.
Those who stay inside the house will be safe; anyone who leaves is responsible for their own fate. Safety is found within the covenant boundary.

f.w: his blood shall be upon his head
f.g: He is responsible for his own death.

chapters.n: If she reveals their mission, the oath is void.
Rahab agrees and immediately ties the scarlet cord in the window — acting on her faith right away.

f.w: According unto your words, so be it

chapters.n: The spies hide three days in the hills while the searchers fail to find them.
They return across the Jordan and report everything to Joshua.
Their report is full of faith, unlike the fearful report of the twelve spies years before: the Lord has given us the land; its people are terrified.

f.w: Truly the LORD hath delivered into our hands all the land

chapters.n: Joshua leads the whole nation from Shittim to the bank of the Jordan, where they camp before crossing. Rising early is a recurring sign of Joshua’s eagerness to obey.
After three days of waiting, the officers pass through the camp with instructions.
When the priests lift the ark, the people must follow it. The ark — symbol of God’s presence — leads the way.
They must keep about 2,000 cubits — roughly 3,000 feet (900 m) — behind it, showing reverence and allowing everyone to see the path through unknown territory.

f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm).

f.w: ye have not passed this way heretofore
f.g: You’ve never been this way before.

chapters.n: “Sanctify yourselves” — prepare spiritually, because tomorrow God will do wonders. Spiritual preparation precedes miracles.

f.g: Make yourselves ritually and spiritually holy.

chapters.n: Joshua instructs the priests to carry the ark ahead of the people, and they obey.
God promises to honor Joshua publicly, showing all Israel that he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses.

f.w: This day will I begin to magnify thee

chapters.n: The priests are to step into the edge of the river and stand there — an act of faith before the miracle happens.

f.w: ye shall stand still in Jordan

chapters.n: Joshua gathers the people to hear God’s word.
The coming miracle will prove the living God is among them and will surely drive out the seven nations of Canaan.
The ark of “the Lord of all the earth” will go ahead into the river. Israel’s God is not a local deity but Lord of the whole earth.

f.w: the Lord of all the earth

chapters.n: One man from each tribe is chosen for a task to be explained in chapter 4.
The promise: as soon as the priests’ feet touch the water, the river upstream will stop and pile up in a heap.

f.w: they shall stand upon an heap

chapters.n: The people break camp and follow, with the priests carrying the ark at the front.
This was spring harvest, when the Jordan overflows its banks from snowmelt — the hardest time to cross. The miracle began only when the priests’ feet got wet.

f.w: Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest

chapters.n: The water stopped far upstream at the town of Adam, while the flow down to the Dead Sea was cut off. Some note that landslides near Adam (modern Damiya) have dammed the Jordan in recorded history — God’s timing remained the miracle.

f.g: A town about 18 miles (30 km) upstream, near modern Damiya.

chapters.n: The priests stood firm in the middle of the riverbed while the whole nation crossed on dry ground — a new generation’s Red Sea crossing.
Once everyone has crossed, the Lord gives Joshua a new instruction. Miracles are meant to be remembered.
Choose twelve men, one from each tribe — every tribe shares in the memorial.

f.w: out of every tribe a man

chapters.n: Each man takes a stone from the exact spot where the priests stood in the riverbed and carries it to that night’s campsite.
Joshua summons the twelve men already chosen.

f.g: Whom he had appointed in advance.

chapters.n: Each man returns into the riverbed, past the ark, and hoists a stone on his shoulder.
The stones are meant to spark questions from children. Memorials invite family teaching.

f.w: when your children ask their fathers

chapters.n: Parents will answer: the river stopped before the ark of the Lord. The stones bear lasting witness. Latter-day Saints use journals, sacrament, and temples similarly as reminders.
The twelve men do exactly as commanded and lay the stones down at the camp.

f.w: as the LORD spake unto Joshua

chapters.n: Joshua also sets up a second circle of twelve stones in the riverbed where the priests stood — visible “unto this day” to the writer’s readers, perhaps at low water.

f.g: A phrase showing the account was written down some time after the events.

chapters.n: The priests held their place in midriver until everything was done, while the people hurried across.
Last of all, the ark and priests crossed in full view of the people.

f.w: in the presence of the people

chapters.n: The eastern tribes kept their promise to Moses, crossing armed ahead of the others.
About 40,000 warriors crossed to the plains of Jericho, ready for battle “before the Lord.”

f.g: In God’s presence, as his army.

chapters.n: God fulfilled his promise: Joshua was honored before Israel, who now respected him as they had Moses.
The Lord speaks again to Joshua.

f.g: Joshua acts only on God’s word.

chapters.n: Command the priests carrying the ark to come up out of the river.

f.g: So called because it held the tablets of the covenant (the “testimony”).

chapters.n: Joshua relays the command.

f.g: Climb up out of the riverbed.

chapters.n: The moment the priests’ feet touched dry land, the waters rushed back to flood level — proof that the river had been held back by God.

f.w: the waters of Jordan returned unto their place

chapters.n: The date: the 10th day of the first month — the very day Passover lambs were chosen. Exactly forty years after leaving Egypt, Israel camps at Gilgal.

f.w: the tenth day of the first month

f.g: Probably “circle” (of stones); Israel’s base camp near Jericho.

chapters.n: Joshua sets up the twelve stones at Gilgal.
He repeats the instruction: when children ask about the stones…
…tell them: Israel crossed this river on dry ground.
God dried up the Jordan just as he did the Red Sea. The two crossings bracket the wilderness era.

f.w: as the LORD your God did to the Red sea

chapters.n: Two purposes: that the whole world will know God’s power, and that Israel will reverence him forever.

f.w: That all the people of the earth might know
the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty

chapters.n: News of the Jordan miracle spreads to the kings west of the river and along the coast. Their courage melts — giving Israel a window of safety to renew its covenant.
God commands that the men be circumcised — a “second time” for the nation, renewing the covenant sign the wilderness generation had neglected.

f.g: Literally “knives of flint” — stone blades used for sacred rites.

chapters.n: Joshua carries out the command at a site nicknamed “the hill of the foreskins.”
The reason: the men who left Egypt had all died during the forty years.
Those who left Egypt were circumcised, but sons born in the wilderness had not been.

f.g: Possibly because of the people’s rebellion and the hardships of travel.

chapters.n: Forty years of wandering came because the Exodus generation disobeyed; God swore they would not see the land.

f.w: because they obeyed not the voice of the LORD

chapters.n: Their children, raised up in their place, received the covenant sign under Joshua. A new generation makes its own covenant.

f.w: whom he raised up in their stead

chapters.n: The men stayed in camp until they healed — a vulnerable moment that required trust in God’s protection, right on the enemy’s doorstep.
God says he has “rolled away” the shame of Egypt. The name Gilgal sounds like the Hebrew word for “roll.” Their slave identity was gone; they were a covenant people.

f.w: I rolled away the reproach of Egypt

chapters.n: Israel keeps its first Passover in the promised land, on the 14th day of the first month at evening — forty years after the first one in Egypt.
The next day they ate produce of the land — unleavened bread and roasted grain — fulfilling God’s promise of a land of plenty.

f.g: Stored grain or produce of the land.

chapters.n: The manna stopped the day after. God’s miraculous provision ends when ordinary means become available — he doesn’t do for us what we can now do ourselves.
Near Jericho, Joshua sees a man with a drawn sword and boldly asks, “Are you with us or against us?”

f.w: his sword drawn in his hand

chapters.n: “Neither” — he is the commander of the Lord’s army. The real question isn’t whether God is on our side, but whether we are on his. Joshua bows in worship.

f.w: captain of the host of the LORD
f.g: Commander of the Lord’s army (of angels).
Bowed down; he accepts the worship, suggesting a divine messenger.

chapters.n: As with Moses at the burning bush, Joshua must remove his sandals on holy ground. Joshua is confirmed as Moses’ successor in sacred experience too.

f.w: Loose thy shoe from off thy foot

chapters.n: Jericho is locked down tight — no one in or out. Its walls seemed impossible to breach without siege engines.
Before any battle, God declares it already done: “I have given Jericho into your hand.” The victory is God’s gift, not Israel’s achievement.

f.w: I have given into thine hand Jericho

chapters.n: The plan is strange: march around the city once a day for six days.
Seven priests with ram’s-horn trumpets go before the ark; on the seventh day, seven circuits. Seven — the number of completeness — runs all through the story.

f.g: Shofars — horns blown at sacred moments.

chapters.n: At the long trumpet blast, everyone shouts, the wall collapses, and each soldier goes straight in.

f.w: the wall of the city shall fall down flat

chapters.n: Joshua relays God’s instructions to the priests.

f.w: Take up the ark of the covenant

chapters.n: The armed men lead the procession ahead of the ark.
The procession begins: trumpeters, then the ark, the visible sign of God’s presence. The ark is called “the Lord” itself here.
Order of march: armed guards, trumpet-priests, the ark, and a rear guard.
The people must stay completely silent until Joshua gives the word. Discipline and trust in silence came before the shout of victory.
Day one: one silent circuit, then back to camp.
Joshua rises early again, eager to obey.
The same procession repeats, with trumpets sounding continuously.
For six days they repeat the same routine. Faith sometimes means doing what God asks day after day without seeing results yet.
On day seven they start at dawn and circle the city seven times.

f.w: about the dawning of the day

chapters.n: On the seventh circuit, Joshua cries, “Shout! The Lord has given you the city!”

f.w: Shout; for the LORD hath given you the city

chapters.n: Jericho is placed under the ban — devoted entirely to the Lord. Only Rahab and her household are spared because of her faith.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — devoted to God, usually by destruction.

f.w: only Rahab the harlot shall live

chapters.n: A strong warning: take nothing from the devoted things, or the whole camp will be cursed. This sets up the tragedy of Achan in chapter 7.

f.w: keep yourselves from the accursed thing

f.g: Bring disaster on it — a word that becomes Achan’s place-name (Achor).

chapters.n: All precious metals belong to the Lord’s treasury — Jericho was a kind of “firstfruits” of the land given to God.
The trumpets sound, the people shout, the wall falls flat, and Israel takes the city. Archaeologists still debate Jericho’s ruins and dating; the text’s focus is on God’s power.
Everything living in the city was destroyed under the ban. Readers today often find this deeply disturbing; the text presents it as divine judgment on Canaanite wickedness.
But Joshua honored the spies’ oath, sending them to bring Rahab out safely.
Rahab and her whole family were rescued and placed outside the camp — at first outside, as they were not yet part of Israel.

f.g: Outside the camp, likely until they were purified.

chapters.n: The city was burned; precious metals went into the Lord’s treasury.

f.w: the treasury of the house of the LORD

chapters.n: Rahab became part of Israel, still living there when the account was written. The Gospel of Matthew names her as an ancestor of Jesus Christ.
Joshua pronounced a curse on anyone who would rebuild Jericho’s fortifications: it would cost him his eldest and youngest sons. Fulfilled in the days of King Ahab.

f.w: Cursed be the man before the LORD, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho

chapters.n: God was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land — fulfilling God’s promise in 1:5.

f.w: So the LORD was with Joshua

chapters.n: The narrator tells us right away what no one in Israel yet knows: one man, Achan, secretly took devoted spoil from Jericho. One person’s hidden sin affected the whole covenant community.
Joshua sends scouts to Ai, a town up in the hills near Bethel.

f.g: “House of God,” where Jacob saw the ladder.

chapters.n: Overconfident after Jericho, the scouts advise sending only a few thousand men — Ai seems small.

f.w: make not all the people to labour thither
f.g: Don’t tire the whole army with the climb.

chapters.n: About three thousand men attack — and run away.

f.w: they fled before the men of Ai

chapters.n: Thirty-six Israelites are killed as they flee down the slope. Now it is Israel whose hearts melt, just as the Canaanites’ had.

f.g: “The quarries” or “breaks” — a place on the descent.

f.w: the hearts of the people melted

chapters.n: Joshua and the elders tear their clothes, fall facedown before the ark until evening, and throw dust on their heads — signs of grief and humiliation.
Joshua’s anguished prayer sounds like the murmuring of the wilderness generation: why did you bring us here? Even great leaders can feel despair.

f.w: would to God we had been content

chapters.n: “What can I say when Israel runs from its enemies?”
He worries the Canaanites will surround and destroy them — and asks, “What will you do for your own great name?” Moses had prayed similarly.

f.w: what wilt thou do unto thy great name

chapters.n: God tells Joshua to stand up — this is not the time for lying on his face. The problem needs action, not just lament.
God reveals the cause: Israel has sinned. Stealing, deceiving, and hiding the devoted things broke the covenant.
Israel’s defeat came because they were now under the ban themselves. God will not be with them until the devoted things are removed.

f.w: neither will I be with you any more

chapters.n: Joshua must prepare the people spiritually: tomorrow the hidden sin will be exposed.
By sacred lot, God will single out the tribe, then the clan, then the household, then the individual.

f.w: the tribe which the LORD taketh
f.g: Chosen by lot, perhaps with the Urim and Thummim.

chapters.n: The guilty person, with everything he has, would be burned — treated as devoted to destruction because he took what was devoted.

f.g: Committed a disgraceful act against the community.

chapters.n: Early the next morning Joshua presents the tribes; Judah is singled out.
Within Judah, the clan of Zerah is taken, then the family of Zabdi.

f.g: Descendants of Zerah, son of Judah.

chapters.n: Then, man by man, Achan is identified. The slow process gave him many chances to come forward on his own.
Joshua speaks gently — “my son” — urging Achan to honor God by telling the truth. Confession is part of repentance.

f.w: give, I pray thee, glory to the LORD
f.g: A formula urging someone to tell the truth under oath.

chapters.n: Achan admits his sin plainly.
He describes a pattern as old as Eden: he saw, he coveted, he took, he hid. A fine robe from Babylonia, silver, and a gold bar were buried under his tent.

f.g: A gold bar, about 1¼ lb (0.6 kg).

chapters.n: Messengers run to the tent and find everything exactly as he described.

f.g: Haste to remove the cause of trouble.

chapters.n: The items are laid out before the Lord — returned to the One they belonged to.

f.w: laid them out before the LORD
f.g: Spread them out in God’s presence.

chapters.n: Achan, his family, possessions, and the stolen goods are taken to a valley. Under ancient notions of corporate responsibility, the household shared in his fate — a hard element of the account.

f.g: Some interpreters think they were complicit, since the loot was hidden in the family tent.

chapters.n: A wordplay: “Why have you troubled (achar) us? The Lord will trouble you.” The judgment is carried out by stoning and fire.
A heap of stones marks the spot, and God’s anger turns away. Yet the prophets later promised that the Valley of Achor would become “a door of hope.”
With the sin removed, God renews his encouragement: don’t be afraid; take the whole army this time. Victory is again declared before the battle.

f.w: Fear not, neither be thou dismayed
I have given into thy hand

chapters.n: Ai would be treated like Jericho, except this time Israel may keep the livestock and goods. Had Achan waited, he could have had plunder lawfully. God also gives a battle plan: an ambush.

f.w: shall ye take for a prey unto yourselves

chapters.n: Joshua selects an elite force and sends them out under cover of night.

f.g: The Hebrew ’elef can mean “thousand” or a military unit, so numbers may be smaller than they look.

chapters.n: They are to hide close behind the city, ready to strike.
Joshua’s main force would approach openly and then pretend to flee, as Israel really had the first time.
The men of Ai, overconfident, would chase them and leave the city.
Then the ambush would rise up and seize the undefended city — with God giving the victory.

f.w: the LORD your God will deliver it

chapters.n: Once taken, the city was to be set on fire as the signal.
The ambush force took position west of Ai, between it and Bethel, while Joshua spent the night with the main army.
Early the next morning, Joshua reviewed the troops and led them with the elders toward Ai.
The main army camped north of Ai, in plain view across a valley.
About five thousand were positioned in the ambush to the west — likely a detail of the same plan in verse 3.

f.g: Scholars debate how this relates to the 30,000 in verse 3.

chapters.n: With everyone in place, Joshua went down into the valley that night, drawing the enemy’s attention.
Ai’s king saw Israel and rushed out at dawn to attack, unaware of the ambush behind him.
Joshua and Israel pretended to be beaten and fled toward the wilderness.

f.w: made as if they were beaten

chapters.n: All Ai’s men were called out to pursue, drawn far from the city.

f.w: were drawn away from the city

chapters.n: Not a man was left in Ai or nearby Bethel; the city gates stood wide open.
God tells Joshua to point his spear (or javelin) at Ai — the signal for the ambush and a sign of God’s power, like Moses’ raised staff.

f.g: Possibly a curved sword or javelin (Hebrew kidon).

chapters.n: At his signal the ambush sprang, entered the city, and set it ablaze.
The men of Ai looked back and saw their city’s smoke rising to the sky — trapped with nowhere to run. Israel’s “fleeing” army turned on them.

f.w: the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven

chapters.n: Seeing the smoke, Joshua and the main force turned and attacked.
The ambush force came out of the city behind them, catching Ai’s army in between.
The king of Ai was captured alive and brought to Joshua.
After the battle in the field, Israel returned and struck the city itself.

f.g: A common idiom for killing in battle.

chapters.n: Twelve thousand people of Ai died that day — the full population of the town.
Joshua kept his spear stretched out until the victory was complete, as Moses had held up his hands against Amalek.

f.w: Joshua drew not his hand back

chapters.n: As God allowed, Israel kept the livestock and plunder.

f.w: according unto the word of the LORD

chapters.n: Ai was burned and left a permanent ruin — fitting its name, “The Heap.”

f.g: Hebrew tel ‘olam — a permanent mound of ruins.

chapters.n: The king’s body was hung up until evening, then taken down before sunset as the law required, and covered with a pile of stones at the city gate.

f.w: as soon as the sun was down

chapters.n: After the victories, Joshua leads Israel north to Mount Ebal near Shechem to renew the covenant — just as Moses commanded. Worship takes priority over further conquest.
He builds the altar exactly as Moses specified — uncut stones — and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings.

f.g: Fellowship sacrifices shared in a meal.

chapters.n: Joshua writes a copy of the law of Moses on the stones before all the people.

f.w: a copy of the law of Moses

chapters.n: All Israel — native-born and foreigners alike — stands in two halves facing Gerizim and Ebal, with the ark and priests in the valley between.

f.w: half of them over against mount Gerizim

chapters.n: Joshua reads the whole law aloud, including the blessings and curses.
Every word was read to the entire assembly — men, women, children, and foreigners. Everyone needed to hear and understand the covenant.
News of Israel’s victories spreads to all the kings west of the Jordan — in the hill country, the lowlands, and along the Mediterranean coast.

f.g: The Shephelah — the low foothills toward the coast.

chapters.n: Normally rival city-states unite to fight Israel together.
But the people of Gibeon, a major city just a few miles from Ai, choose a different strategy.

f.g: A Hivite city about 6 miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: They act cleverly, disguising themselves as envoys from far away, with worn-out sacks and cracked, patched wineskins. The word “wilily” echoes Israel’s own trickery at Ai.
Worn and patched sandals, ragged clothes, and dry, crumbly bread complete the costume.
At Israel’s camp in Gilgal they claim to come from a distant land and ask for a treaty.

f.w: make ye a league with us

chapters.n: Israel is suspicious: what if you live nearby? The law forbade treaties with Canaanite peoples.

f.w: how shall we make a league with you

chapters.n: The Gibeonites humbly call themselves Joshua’s servants. Joshua asks directly who they are and where they’re from.
They say they came because of the fame of Israel’s God — mentioning only events far in the past, like Egypt, wisely leaving out recent Jericho and Ai.

f.w: because of the name of the LORD thy God

chapters.n: They mention the defeat of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan — old news a distant people might have heard.
They claim their elders sent them with provisions to offer submission and seek a treaty.
“This bread was warm from the oven when we left — look at it now.”
“These wineskins were new, and our clothes and shoes have worn out on the long journey.”

f.w: by reason of the very long journey
f.g: A clever lie supported by props.

chapters.n: Israel’s leaders sampled the provisions but did not ask the Lord for guidance — the critical mistake. Appearances can deceive; revelation does not.

f.w: asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD

chapters.n: Joshua made peace with them, and the leaders swore an oath to spare their lives.
Three days later the truth came out: they were close neighbors.
Israel arrived at their four cities on the third day — all within a day’s march.

f.g: Later the resting place of the ark for twenty years.

chapters.n: Israel didn’t attack, because the leaders had sworn by the Lord. The people grumbled, but an oath in God’s name was binding.

f.w: sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel

chapters.n: The leaders stood firm: we swore by the Lord, so we can’t harm them.
Breaking the oath would bring God’s wrath. Centuries later, when Saul violated it, Israel suffered famine.
Their lives were spared, but they became woodcutters and water carriers for the community.

f.w: hewers of wood and drawers of water

chapters.n: Joshua confronts them: Why did you deceive us?

f.g: Possibly near Qumran, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found.

chapters.n: En-gedi, a lush spring in the desert cliffs above the Dead Sea, became a famous hiding place and garden spot.

f.g: Location uncertain; near the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: An honest note: Judah could not take Jerusalem. It stayed Jebusite until David captured it centuries later. The phrase “unto this day” shows the writer lived before David’s conquest.

f.g: Up to the time the book was written.

chapters.n: The tribes descended from Joseph receive the central hill country, the heart of the land. Their southern border begins at the Jordan near Jericho and climbs toward Bethel.

f.g: The spring at Jericho, today called Elisha’s Spring.

chapters.n: The line runs past Bethel and Luz. Bethel is where Jacob saw the ladder to heaven; Luz was its older name or a neighboring town.

f.g: The home clan of Hushai the Archite, David’s friend.

chapters.n: The border goes down the western slopes past Lower Beth-horon and Gezer to the Mediterranean.

f.g: In KJV English “coast” usually means border or territory, not seashore.

chapters.n: Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, each became a full tribe, so Joseph received a double portion — the birthright blessing.
Now Ephraim’s own borders are traced. Its land ran from the Bethel area north to about Shechem.

f.g: Upper Beth-horon, on the ridge above the valley of Aijalon.

chapters.n: The northern edge runs from Michmethah, near Shechem, east toward the Jordan valley.

f.g: A site southeast of Shechem; not the city of Shiloh itself.

chapters.n: The eastern line drops down into the Jordan valley near Jericho, closing the outline of Ephraim.

f.g: “Crowns”; a common town name in the region.

chapters.n: On the west, the brook Kanah separates Ephraim from Manasseh as it flows to the sea.

f.g: Probably the Wadi Qanah, a seasonal stream flowing west into the Yarkon.

chapters.n: Some Ephraimite towns lay inside Manasseh’s area. The brother tribes’ land was interwoven, as their history would be.

f.g: Towns set apart for Ephraim though located in Manasseh’s territory.

chapters.n: Ephraim left the Canaanites in Gezer and made them pay forced labor instead. This half-obedience becomes a pattern that Judges shows bearing bitter fruit.

f.g: Were made to do forced labor or pay tribute.

chapters.n: Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, had already received Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan through Machir’s clan, known for its warriors.
The rest of Manasseh’s clans receive land west of the Jordan. Shechem here is a clan name that also became a city name.
Zelophehad had only daughters. Without sons, his family’s name and land could have vanished from Israel.
The five sisters remind the leaders of the Lord’s earlier ruling through Moses, and they receive their land. Their faith and courage changed Israel’s law to protect families like theirs.

f.g: Aaron’s son and successor as high priest.

chapters.n: Manasseh’s western land is divided into ten shares, in addition to the eastern lands across the Jordan.

f.g: Five for the five clans and five for Zelophehad’s daughters (one clan, Hepher, being represented by them).

chapters.n: This explains the ten shares: the daughters counted alongside the sons, while the Machir clan already held Gilead.

f.g: Here meaning Zelophehad’s daughters, female descendants of Manasseh.

chapters.n: Manasseh’s southern border runs from near Shechem toward En-tappuah. “On the right hand” means to the south, since directions were given facing east.

f.g: Facing east (the Hebrew way of orienting), the right hand is south.

chapters.n: The town of Tappuah sat on the boundary: its land belonged to Manasseh, but the town itself to Ephraim — an example of the tribes’ overlapping holdings.
The brook Kanah marks the line between the two tribes down to the sea, with some Ephraimite towns north of it.

f.g: The end point of a border line.

chapters.n: Manasseh’s land touches Asher in the northwest and Issachar in the northeast, spreading across the central hills to the sea.
Manasseh was also given strong Canaanite cities in the plains, including Megiddo and Beth-shean, which guarded key trade routes.

f.g: A fortress city overlooking the Jezreel valley; its name lies behind “Armageddon.”

chapters.n: Manasseh could not take these cities, and the Canaanites stayed. Iron chariots on the open plains made them hard to defeat.
When Israel grew strong, they chose to make the Canaanites pay tribute rather than finish the work. Profit replaced obedience.
Joseph’s tribes complain that their share is too small for so large a people. They ask for more without wanting to do the hard work.
Joshua — himself an Ephraimite — answers with gentle irony: if you are so great, clear the forests and take the land the Lord already gave you.

f.g: The forested hill country, then still largely uncleared.
One of the peoples living in Canaan, perhaps villagers of the open country.

chapters.n: They object: the hills are too small, and the plains are held by Canaanites with iron chariots. They see the obstacles more than the promise.

f.g: Chariots with iron fittings, the most advanced weapons of the day.
The broad fertile plain in northern Israel.

chapters.n: Joshua turns their boast into a challenge: yes, you are great and powerful, so you will have more than one portion — if you act on that strength.
Joshua promises they will clear the forest and drive out the Canaanites, chariots and all. God’s gifts often come as opportunities that require effort and faith.

f.g: Clear the forest for farming and settlement.

chapters.n: Israel moves the tabernacle to Shiloh in the central hills, where it would stay through the time of the judges until Samuel’s day. The house of God now has a settled home in the land.

f.g: The portable sanctuary, also called the tent of meeting.

chapters.n: Seven tribes still had no land. The major battles were over, but the work of settling had stalled.

f.g: Benjamin, Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Dan.

chapters.n: Joshua gently rebukes them for hesitating to take what God had already given. Receiving a promised blessing still takes action.
Joshua organizes a survey party — three men from each tribe — so that every tribe has a fair voice in mapping the land.

f.g: Write a survey or description of it, like drawing up a map.

chapters.n: Judah in the south and Joseph in the center keep their portions; the remaining land is to be split into seven parts.
The surveyors are to bring their written description back so Joshua can cast lots “before the Lord,” trusting Him to make the final assignment.
The Levites receive no territory because their inheritance is the priesthood itself. The two and a half eastern tribes already have their land.

f.w: the priesthood of the LORD is their inheritance

chapters.n: Joshua gives the surveyors their charge. Walking the land was itself a way of claiming it, echoing God’s command to Abraham.
The men divide the land city by city into seven sections and record it in a book. Careful records served justice and kept the peace among tribes.

f.g: A written scroll; one of the earliest mentions of a land survey in scripture.

chapters.n: Joshua casts the lots in Shiloh before the Lord. Each tribe’s land came as a gift from God, not as a prize seized by the strongest.

f.g: In the presence of the tabernacle, the place of God’s presence.

chapters.n: Benjamin’s lot falls between Judah and Joseph, a small but strategic strip. Moses had blessed Benjamin as one who dwells safely beside the Lord.
The northern border starts at the Jordan, runs past Jericho, and climbs into the hills to the wilderness of Beth-aven.

f.g: Means “house of wickedness”; prophets later used it mockingly for Bethel.

chapters.n: The line passes south of Bethel and descends to Ataroth-adar near Lower Beth-horon.
The western border runs south to Kirjath-jearim, which belonged to Judah.
Benjamin’s southern border begins at Kirjath-jearim — the same line as Judah’s northern border traced in reverse.
The line runs along the valley of Hinnom just south of the Jebusite city, placing Jerusalem itself inside Benjamin.

f.g: Hebrew valley of Rephaim, southwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: From the springs near Jerusalem the border runs east down the steep road toward Jericho.

f.g: “Red places,” the red-rock ascent on the Jerusalem–Jericho road, traditional setting of the Good Samaritan parable.

chapters.n: The border descends into the Arabah, the deep rift valley of the Jordan.

f.g: The rift valley running from the Sea of Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba.

chapters.n: Benjamin’s southern border ends at the north shore of the Dead Sea where the Jordan enters.
The Jordan forms the eastern side, completing Benjamin’s outline.
The towns of Benjamin’s eastern district begin with Jericho, the first city taken in Canaan.
Bethel is listed in Benjamin here, though it later became an Ephraimite and northern-kingdom shrine.
Ophrah in Benjamin is different from Gideon’s Ophrah in Manasseh.
Gaba (Geba) later became a key frontier post on Benjamin’s northern edge. The eastern district totals twelve cities.
The western district begins with Gibeon, whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty, and Ramah, the later home of Samuel.
Mizpeh of Benjamin became a gathering place for Israel’s assemblies under Samuel.
Three small towns of Benjamin, otherwise unknown today.
Zelah held the tomb of Saul’s family; Gibeath is Gibeah, Saul’s hometown; and Jerusalem is assigned to Benjamin though not yet conquered.
Simeon’s land lies inside Judah’s southern territory. This fulfills Jacob’s deathbed words that Simeon would be scattered within Israel.

f.w: within the inheritance of the children of Judah

chapters.n: Simeon’s towns begin with Beer-sheba, the famous well of the patriarchs.

f.g: Possibly a copying slip; 1 Chronicles 4:28 omits it.

chapters.n: These towns also appear in Judah’s list, showing the two tribes shared the same region.
Hormah, “destruction,” was the site of early battles in the wilderness period.
Beth-marcaboth means “house of chariots” and Hazar-susah “village of horses” — perhaps depots on the road to Egypt.
Sharuhen was a fortified town near Gaza. This group totals thirteen cities.

f.g: Known from Egyptian records as a stronghold in southwestern Canaan.

chapters.n: Four more towns, some lying in the foothills rather than the far south.
Simeon also held the villages around these towns as far as Baalath-beer, the “high place of the south.”

f.g: “Height of the Negev”; possibly the Ramoth of 1 Samuel 30:27.

chapters.n: Judah’s portion was larger than it needed, so Simeon was settled inside it. Over time Simeon largely blended into Judah.

f.g: More than Judah needed or could occupy.

chapters.n: Zebulun’s lot is in Lower Galilee, between the Jezreel valley and the hills of Nazareth.

f.g: A town on Zebulun’s southern border, near the Jezreel valley.

chapters.n: The border runs west toward the brook by Jokneam at the foot of Mount Carmel.
Eastward the line runs to the slopes of Mount Tabor. Japhia lies near later Nazareth.
Gath-hepher is the hometown of the prophet Jonah.
The northern edge reaches Hannathon and the valley of Jiphthah-el.
This Bethlehem is a small Galilean town, not Bethlehem of Judah, the birthplace of David and of Jesus.

f.g: Bethlehem of Zebulun, northwest of Nazareth; possibly the home of the judge Ibzan.

chapters.n: Zebulun’s land, small but fertile, lay in the region later called Galilee, where Jesus would grow up and teach.
Issachar’s lot covers the eastern Jezreel valley, rich farmland between Mount Tabor and the Jordan.
Jezreel, Chesulloth, and Shunem lie in the great valley. Shunem was home to the woman who hosted Elisha.
More towns in Issachar’s fertile plain.
Kishion was later given to the Levites.
En-gannim, “spring of gardens,” lay on Issachar’s southern edge.
The border reaches Mount Tabor and the Jordan. Tabor is where Barak gathered Israel to fight Sisera.

f.g: A northern “house of the sun,” different from the one in Judah.

chapters.n: Issachar’s inheritance totals sixteen towns with their villages.
Asher receives the coastal strip in the northwest, from Mount Carmel north toward Sidon.
Asher’s border towns begin in the plain of Acco.
The border reaches Mount Carmel on the west, the ridge where Elijah later confronted the prophets of Baal.
The line turns east toward Zebulun. “On the left hand” means north, since directions were given facing east.

f.g: Facing east, the left hand is north.

chapters.n: Asher’s territory stretches toward “great Zidon,” the major Phoenician port. This Hebron is a northern town, not Caleb’s city.

f.g: Sidon, chief city of the Phoenicians.

chapters.n: The border reaches the fortress city of Tyre. These coastal cities stayed Phoenician; Asher never controlled them.
Asher’s cities total twenty-two. This Aphek lies in the north, near Acco.
Asher’s inheritance is summed up, though Judges will show much of it remained in Canaanite hands.
Naphtali receives the mountainous north, west of the Sea of Galilee and the upper Jordan.
Naphtali’s border includes the great oak of Zaanannim, where Jael’s tent would later stand.
Naphtali’s land touches Zebulun, Asher, and the Jordan. “Judah upon Jordan” is puzzling; it may refer to a place name or be an early copying change.

f.g: Unclear; the Greek Septuagint omits “Judah” here.

chapters.n: Fortified cities on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Chinnereth gave the lake its old name.

f.g: The Sea of Galilee was called the Sea of Chinnereth (“harp-shaped”).

chapters.n: Hazor, the great northern city that Joshua burned, falls within Naphtali’s land.
Kedesh became a city of refuge and the hometown of Barak.
Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh, named for Canaanite deities, remained partly Canaanite.
Naphtali’s inheritance — nineteen cities — is complete. Isaiah later prophesied a great light dawning over this northern land.
Dan, last to receive land, gets a small region west of Benjamin toward the coast.
Zorah and Eshtaol are the hometown area of Samson, a Danite.
Ajalon (Aijalon) is the valley where the sun stood still in Joshua’s battle.
Thimnathah is Timnah, home of Samson’s Philistine bride. Ekron was a Philistine city.
Gibbethon later fell into Philistine hands and was besieged by Israel’s kings.
Towns near modern Tel Aviv. Bene-berak preserves the name of today’s Bnei Brak.

f.g: “Sons of lightning”; the name survives in modern Bnei Brak.

chapters.n: Dan’s land reaches the Yarkon River and the area of Joppa, the port where Jonah later took ship.
Squeezed by Amorites and Philistines, Dan could not hold its land and moved north, capturing Leshem (Laish) and renaming it Dan. Judges 18 tells the story.

f.g: Proved too small, or slipped from their grasp.

chapters.n: A closing line summarizes Dan’s original allotment before the migration north.
Only after every tribe has its portion does Joshua receive his own. The leader takes his inheritance last, a quiet mark of humble service.
Joshua receives Timnath-serah in Ephraim’s hills, as the Lord directed, and builds it up. He was buried there.
The division is finished at Shiloh at the tabernacle door, under priest, prophet-leader, and tribal heads together. God’s promise to the patriarchs now has a map.
With the land divided, the Lord gives Joshua instructions to set up a justice system. Settling the land includes protecting human life.

f.w: The LORD also spake unto Joshua

chapters.n: The Lord reminds Israel of the cities of refuge He had already commanded through Moses. Now it is time to name them.

f.g: Through Moses as the Lord’s messenger.

chapters.n: A person who killed someone by accident could flee to a refuge city for protection from the victim’s relative seeking revenge. God’s law distinguished accident from murder.

f.g: Hebrew go’el, the nearest kinsman, responsible for avenging a family member’s death.

chapters.n: The fugitive explains his case to the elders at the city gate, the usual place of judgment. If they accept it, they take him in and give him a place to live.

f.g: City gates were where elders met to hear cases.

chapters.n: The city must not hand him over to the avenger, because the death was not planned and came from no prior hatred.

f.g: Had no earlier hostility toward him.

chapters.n: He stays until his case is formally judged and until the high priest dies; then he may go home in safety. Many see in this a picture of how the death of a High Priest — Christ — sets the guilty free.

f.w: until the death of the high priest

f.g: Face a formal hearing by the community.

chapters.n: Three refuge cities are named west of the Jordan — north, center, and south — so that no one was ever too far from safety.
Three more refuge cities lie east of the Jordan, which Moses had already chosen.
The cities protected both Israelites and foreigners living among them. God’s mercy and fair hearing extended to the stranger too.

f.g: A foreign resident living among Israel.

chapters.n: The leaders of the Levite families come to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads to claim what the Lord had promised them.
They remind Israel that Moses commanded cities be given to the Levites, with pastureland for their animals. Like Zelophehad’s daughters, they ask on the basis of God’s word.

f.g: Pasturelands around a town, not suburbs in the modern sense.

chapters.n: Israel obeys, giving cities out of each tribe’s land. Supporting those who served at the sanctuary was a shared responsibility.

f.w: at the commandment of the LORD

chapters.n: The priests — Aaron’s descendants, from the Kohath branch of Levi — draw first and receive thirteen cities near the future site of the temple in Jerusalem.

f.g: The priests proper, as distinct from other Levites.

chapters.n: The other Kohathite families receive ten cities in the central tribes.

f.w: rest of the children of Kohath
f.g: Kohathite Levites who were not descendants of Aaron.

chapters.n: The Gershonites receive thirteen cities in the north.
The Merarites receive twelve cities, mostly east of the Jordan and in Zebulun.
Spreading the Levites throughout Israel put teachers of the law in every region, fulfilling Jacob’s word that Levi would be scattered — now turned into a blessing.
The first named cities come from Judah and Simeon.

f.g: The list follows, parallel to 1 Chronicles 6:54-81.

chapters.n: Aaron’s descendants received the first lot — fitting for those who served at the altar.
Hebron becomes a priestly city, the town itself with its pastures.
The fields and villages around Hebron still belonged to Caleb, so his promised inheritance was honored while the priests lived in the town.
Hebron is also a city of refuge. Libnah is the next priestly city.
Two more priestly cities in Judah’s hill country.
Debir, the city Othniel conquered, is also given to the priests.
Beth-shemesh was a priestly town; later its people looked into the ark irreverently and were struck. Nine cities total from Judah and Simeon.
From Benjamin come Gibeon and Geba. Gibeon later hosted the tabernacle in Solomon’s day.
Anathoth was later the home of the priest Abiathar and of the prophet Jeremiah.
The priests receive thirteen cities in all, clustered around what would become Jerusalem.

f.g: Aaron’s line, who officiated at the altar.

chapters.n: The rest of the Kohathites receive towns from Ephraim.
Shechem, a city of refuge, and Gezer are given to the Levites. Gezer was still largely Canaanite.
Two more Ephraimite cities, making four.
From Dan come Eltekeh and Gibbethon.
Aijalon and Gath-rimmon complete Dan’s four.
Two cities from western Manasseh. Gath-rimmon here may be a copying repeat; 1 Chronicles 6:70 has Bileam (Ibleam).
The non-priestly Kohathites receive ten cities in all.
The Gershonites receive Golan in Bashan, a city of refuge, and Beesh-terah east of the Jordan.
From Issachar come four Levite cities in the Jezreel valley region.
Jarmuth here is a northern town, not the southern city of Joshua 10.
Asher gives Mishal and Abdon to the Gershonites.
Rehob, in Asher’s land, was a town the tribe did not fully control.
Naphtali gives Kedesh, a city of refuge, and two others.
The Gershonites receive thirteen cities in total.
The Merarites, the last Levite branch, receive towns from Zebulun.
Nahalal is likely the same as Nahallal of Zebulun’s list.
From Reuben, east of the Dead Sea, come Bezer — a city of refuge — and Jahazah. Some Hebrew manuscripts lack this verse and the next, but other sources and 1 Chronicles include them.
Two more Reubenite cities on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea.
From Gad come Ramoth-gilead, a city of refuge, and Mahanaim, where Jacob saw angels and where David later took refuge from Absalom.
Heshbon was Sihon’s former capital; Jazer was a fertile region east of the Jordan.
The Merarites receive twelve cities.
Forty-eight Levite cities in all — exactly as Moses had commanded. Every tribe hosted the Lord’s servants.
Each city came with pastureland around it, so the Levites could keep herds while serving the people.
A grand summary: the Lord kept His oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Israel now lived in the land promised centuries before.

f.w: which he sware to give unto their fathers

chapters.n: The Lord gave rest from enemies. Even though some Canaanites remained, none could stand against Israel while it trusted God.
A beloved testimony: not one good thing God promised failed. Solomon later echoed these words, and they invite every believer to trust God’s word.
Joshua calls together the two and a half tribes whose land lay east of the Jordan. They had crossed over to help their brothers conquer Canaan.
Joshua praises them for keeping their promise to Moses and following his own orders faithfully.
For years they had fought beside the other tribes instead of going home. Their loyalty kept Israel united.

f.g: Carried out the duty entrusted to them.

chapters.n: With the land at rest, Joshua releases them to go home to their families across the Jordan.

f.g: Go home (an idiom from Israel’s tent-dwelling days).

chapters.n: Joshua’s parting charge sums up the whole law: love God, walk in His ways, keep His commandments, cling to Him, and serve Him with all your heart. Distance from the tabernacle must not mean distance from God.

f.w: to love the LORD your God

f.g: Hold fast to Him, as in a close bond.

chapters.n: Joshua gives them a blessing as they leave, as a father would to departing sons.

f.g: A formal spoken blessing invoking God’s favor.

chapters.n: The text explains that Manasseh was split: half had land in Bashan from Moses, half west of the Jordan from Joshua. Joshua blesses the eastern half too.
They return rich with spoil and are told to share it with those who stayed home — a principle of fairness already set by Moses and later by David.
The eastern tribes leave Shiloh and head toward Gilead, their land east of the Jordan.

f.g: The highlands east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: At the Jordan they build a huge altar, built to be seen from far away. Its purpose isn’t yet explained, which sets up the crisis that follows.

f.w: a great altar to see to
f.g: An altar impressive to look at — conspicuous.

chapters.n: News spreads to the other tribes that an altar has been built at the river crossing, on the border of Canaan.
The western tribes gather to go to war. The law allowed only one altar for sacrifice, so a second altar looked like rebellion against God.

f.w: to go up to war against them

chapters.n: Wisely, they first send a delegation led by Phinehas, the zealous priest who had once stopped a plague by standing for the Lord.
Ten leaders, one from each western tribe, go with Phinehas, so the whole nation speaks together.

f.g: The clans or military divisions of Israel.

chapters.n: The delegation reaches Gilead and confronts the eastern tribes face to face. Talking first prevents a needless war.
The delegates accuse them of turning from the Lord by building a rival altar.

f.g: Hebrew ma‘al, a breach of faith, betraying a trust.

chapters.n: They recall the sin at Peor, where Israel worshiped Baal and a plague followed. They fear history repeating.
Israel saw itself as one covenant people; one group’s rebellion could bring God’s judgment on all.
They make a generous offer: if your land feels spiritually unclean, come live with us near the tabernacle — just don’t build a rival altar.

f.g: Ritually impure; lacking the Lord’s sanctuary.
The land west of the Jordan, where the tabernacle stood.

chapters.n: They recall Achan, whose secret sin brought defeat on all Israel. One person’s choices can affect the whole community.

f.g: Things devoted to God that were forbidden to be taken.

chapters.n: The eastern tribes answer the leaders.
They make a solemn oath, calling on God twice by three titles: God knows our hearts. If we rebelled, don’t spare us.

f.g: Hebrew El, Elohim, Yahweh — three names for God, repeated for emphasis.

chapters.n: They insist the altar was never meant for sacrifices; if it were, let the Lord Himself punish them.

f.g: A grain offering; “meat” in KJV often means food in general.

chapters.n: Their real fear: someday the western tribes’ children might say the eastern tribes have no part in the Lord.

f.w: What have ye to do with the LORD God of Israel?
f.g: That is, “You aren’t really part of God’s people.”

chapters.n: The Jordan River could become a spiritual dividing line. They worried their children might be shut out and stop fearing the Lord.

f.g: Stop worshiping and revering the Lord.

chapters.n: So they built an altar not to use, but as a monument.
The altar stands as a witness that they also belong to the Lord and will worship at His true sanctuary.
It is a replica, a “pattern” of the Lord’s altar, so future generations can point to it as proof of their shared faith.
They firmly reject any thought of building a competing place of sacrifice. They honor the one altar before the tabernacle.

f.g: An emphatic “Far be it from us!”

chapters.n: Phinehas and the leaders are satisfied. A careful hearing turned suspicion into understanding.

f.g: Literally, “it was good in their eyes.”

chapters.n: Phinehas rejoices that the Lord is still with Israel; the eastern tribes have kept the whole nation safe from judgment.
The delegation returns and reports back to the tribes at Shiloh.
Israel praises God and drops plans for war. Conflict was avoided because people listened before acting.
The eastern tribes name the altar “Witness”: a reminder that the Lord is God for both sides of the Jordan.

f.g: Hebrew “witness.” The word is missing in many Hebrew manuscripts and supplied by translators.

chapters.n: Years after the conquest, Joshua has grown very old. Like Moses and Jacob before him, he prepares farewell counsel.
Joshua summons all of Israel’s leaders. His words are meant to shape the nation after he is gone.

f.g: Respected senior men who governed clans and towns.
Officials who carried out decisions, perhaps scribes or administrators.

chapters.n: Joshua points them to the main lesson of his life: the Lord fought for Israel. Victories came from God, not from their own strength.

f.w: the LORD your God is he that hath fought for you

chapters.n: Joshua has divided even the unconquered areas among the tribes. The job of possessing them now belongs to each tribe.
God promises to drive out the remaining nations — a promise that still depended on Israel’s faithfulness, as Judges will show.
Joshua repeats the charge God once gave him: be very courageous and obey the whole law, not drifting right or left. Courage is needed for obedience, not just battle.
Avoid mixing with the remaining nations’ religion — don’t speak of their gods, swear by them, serve them, or bow to them. Idolatry often begins with small familiarity.

f.w: make mention of the name of their gods

chapters.n: The heart of the message: hold fast to the Lord, as you have done so far.
God has driven out great and strong nations; no one has been able to stand against Israel.

f.w: no man hath been able to stand before you

chapters.n: With God on their side, one Israelite could put a thousand to flight. Strength comes from the Lord, not numbers.

f.w: One man of you shall chase a thousand

chapters.n: Joshua says, in effect, “Guard your own hearts.” Loving the Lord is the safeguard behind all obedience.

f.g: Be very careful; literally “guard your souls.”

chapters.n: Joshua warns against turning back and intermarrying with the remaining nations, which would draw Israel’s hearts toward their gods.
If they compromise, God will stop driving those nations out. Instead, those peoples will become traps, whips, and thorns until Israel loses the land.
Joshua says he is about to die — “going the way of all the earth.” His final testimony: every good promise of God has been fulfilled.

f.w: the way of all the earth

chapters.n: The sober flip side: the same faithful God will also keep His warnings. Covenant blessings and curses are both certain.
Breaking the covenant by serving other gods would kindle the Lord’s anger and cost them the land. The later exiles to Assyria and Babylon fulfilled this warning.
Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem, rich with memory: Abraham built his first altar there, Jacob buried idols there, and Israel had renewed the covenant there under Joshua.

f.g: As in a formal covenant assembly in God’s presence.

chapters.n: Joshua speaks for the Lord, beginning with Israel’s roots: Abraham’s family once worshiped idols beyond the Euphrates. Israel’s story starts with God calling people out of idolatry.

f.w: the other side of the flood
f.g: Beyond the River — the Euphrates, in Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: God took Abraham, led him through Canaan, and gave him Isaac, the long-promised son.
God gave Isaac twin sons. Esau received Mount Seir, while Jacob’s family went down to Egypt.
The Lord sent Moses and Aaron and struck Egypt with plagues, then brought Israel out.
Pharaoh’s chariots chased Israel to the Red Sea.
When Israel cried out, God put darkness between them and the Egyptians and drowned the pursuers. Some of Joshua’s listeners had seen it as children.
God gave Israel victory over the Amorite kings east of the Jordan.
Balak, king of Moab, hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel.
The Lord turned the curse into a blessing. No one can curse whom God has blessed.
After crossing the Jordan, Israel faced Jericho and the seven nations of Canaan, and God gave them all into Israel’s hand.
God sent “the hornet” — perhaps panic or some force that drove the enemy out. The point: victory came not by sword or bow but by God.

f.g: Possibly literal, or a figure for terror sent by God.

chapters.n: Israel enjoys cities, vineyards, and olive groves they never built or planted. Everything they have is a gift of grace.

f.w: a land for which ye did not labour

chapters.n: Now Joshua calls for a response: revere the Lord, serve Him sincerely and faithfully, and get rid of the old idols some still kept.
Joshua’s famous challenge: if serving the Lord seems wrong to you, choose today whom you will serve. Then he declares his own family’s choice. Agency is God’s gift, but neutrality is not an option.

f.w: choose you this day whom ye will serve
as for me and my house
f.g: A beloved motto for families who commit to the Lord together.

chapters.n: The people respond strongly: never would we abandon the Lord for other gods.
They give their reason: the Lord rescued them from slavery in Egypt and protected them all the way.
Because God drove out their enemies, they too will serve Him — “for he is our God.”
Joshua startles them: “You cannot serve the Lord!” He means they cannot serve Him lightly or halfway. A holy God demands full loyalty and will not overlook unrepented rebellion.

f.g: Not petty envy but passionate, exclusive covenant love.
He will not simply ignore covenant betrayal; compare the call to repentance in D&C 58:42-43.

chapters.n: If they turn to other gods, the God who blessed them will bring judgment instead.
The people insist again: “No — we will serve the Lord.”
Joshua makes them witnesses against themselves. Their own word will testify if they break their promise.
Joshua says: then prove it — put away your idols and turn your hearts toward the Lord. True commitment requires action.

f.g: Bend your heart toward; give your whole will.

chapters.n: The people promise a third time to serve and obey the Lord.
Joshua formalizes the covenant, setting statutes and ordinances for the people at Shechem.
Joshua writes the covenant in the book of the law and sets up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary — a visible memorial.
The stone becomes a witness, as if it had heard every word. Each time Israel saw it, they would remember their promise.

f.w: this stone shall be a witness

chapters.n: Joshua sends the people home to their inheritances.
Joshua dies at 110 — the same age as Joseph. Once “Moses’ minister,” he is now honored as “the servant of the Lord,” the title given Moses.
He is buried on his own land at Timnath-serah in Ephraim’s hills.
Israel stayed faithful while Joshua and the elders who had personally seen God’s works were alive. The next verses in Judges show what happened when that generation passed.
Joseph’s bones, carried out of Egypt as he requested, are finally buried at Shechem on land Jacob had bought. A promise made centuries earlier is kept.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son and high priest, also dies and is buried on his son Phinehas’s land. The founding generation’s leaders are gone; the book closes on a generation in transition.
